To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) training parameters of approximate models to maximize likelihood is not appropriate, and that (2) training parameters to minimize empirical risk can be accomplished by back-propagating gradients of approximate inference and decoding errors.

the usual practice of optimizing approximate MAP parameters can result in poor performance, that the parameters that minimize empirical risk can be found using stochastic gradient descent, and that doing so can signicantly reduce loss on test data.

the parameters of an imperfect graphical model should be chosen to minimize its empirical risk, rather than its training loss; and that this can be done efficiently with stochastic back propagation and metadescent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the parameters of graphical models can be trained using the usual empirical risk minimization framework.
the following problem: given a graphical model with approximate inference and prediction, how should we train the parameters of this model?
the following question: how can one train the parameters of graphical models when one does not have access to exact inference?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have shown that the risk minimization approach is a promising alternative to likelihood maximization for learning parameters of graphical models with imperfect inference, decoding, and topology.
the proposed approach is an interesting alternative to the usual way of training graphical models.
the usual way of training graphical models, namely, to approximately maximize the training likelihood, is not optimal.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the empirical risk of a graphical model system should be optimized, and that this can be done using backpropagation.
we have developed a new method to train graphical model parameters, which is more principled and more effective.
, when the goal is accurate prediction, it is better to use approximate inference and decoding, and then to train the parameters of the graphical model using empirical risk minimization.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for a graphical model, it is not enough to simply choose a good approximate inference algorithm.
the empirical risk of a graphical model should be optimized, and not the likelihood of its parameters.
it is often more important to optimize the entire system than to optimize the individual components in isolation.
